text: Volume 3 in the following list. • Volume 1: Summary of Offshore Oil and Gas Well Monitoring Systems and Process Power Requirements (Grelle, Lajeunesse, et al. 2025a) • Volume 2: Generic OTEC Numerical Model for Offshore Oil and Gas Application (Grelle, Lajeunesse and Grendelli, et al. 2025b) • Volume 3: Collocation of OTEC with Offshore Oil and Gas Activities This report presents a synthesis of analyses performed in the overall study and presents concepts of OTEC plants attached to floating offshore oil and gas facilities. The focus of this study was to assess the feasibility and approximate cost of such a system in light of the theoretical synergies that it could have. Additionally, the emphasis of this study was on systems that are currently available on the market, including the types of oil and gas facilities as well as components comprising an OTEC plant design, such as intake water pipes, heat exchangers, turbines, and so on. It should be noted that, while every effort was made to accurately reflect the available components and their costs, as well as the cost of hypothetical installation and operation of an OTEC plant coupled with an oil and gas facility, the authors recognize the many limitations in our understanding of these systems as OTEC is not yet a widely commercially operational concept. Therefore, the reader is urged to treat the findings presented in this report as theoretical case studies aimed at presenting an order-of-magnitude assessment. 1 OESI 2.0 M-1 T-1-P1.1 – Objective 3 Report April 2025 2 Background This research study is funded by the Ocean Energy Safety Institute (OESI) 2.0, a research and development consortium focused on increasing the energy security of the United States, enabling jobs and increased economic activity through responsible and sustainable ocean energy production; developing knowledge, technologies, and training aiding improvements in the safe and sustainable offshore resource production. OESI aims to accomplish these goals through collaboration with industry, research and development institutions, and standards and policy stakeholders. This project aligns with the OESI 2.0 Marine Energy track focused on the small-scale marine energy mapping with other offshore energy and resource development activities. This report is part of a larger research effort that aims to assess the technoeconomic feasibility of deploying anthropogenic GHG emissions (primarily methane) monitoring systems powered with small scale renewable power sources on the Outer Continental Shelf. The larger study has three objectives:  Objective 1 is to summarize the oil and gas equipment monitoring systems and approaches available for the OCS;  Objective 2 is to model a renewable marine energy source (the ocean thermal energy conversion or OTEC was chosen for this study) suitable for deployment on the OCS; and  Objective 3 is to model the collocation of renewable OTEC power sources with offshore oil and gas activities. Objective 3 also focuses on characterizing offshore facilities’ power demand, which can be offset through OTEC power production.
